title: Biomimetic 4D Printing via Poisson Compression Theory: Shifting from Additive Manufacturing to Tension-Driven Poroelastic Self-Assembly
content: Current additive manufacturing (AM) and 3D bioprinting technologies are fundamentally constrained by the "additive" paradigm of layer-by-layer deposition. This approach can limit continuous mechanical anisotropy and may increase fabrication time. In contrast, human fetal morphogenesis achieves the construction of highly anisotropic, complex membranous networks (fasciae) and frictionless internal gliding planes through a fundamentally different physical mechanism. This perspective paper translates the biological "Poisson Compression Theory (PCT)" into novel algorithmic directions for manufacturing. We propose that by treating hydrogels and bio-inks as poroelastic solids and applying macroscopic boundary constraints (e.g., peripheral anchors and drainage vents) combined with internal expansive forces (e.g., stimuli-responsive swelling), materials can autonomously self-assemble via controlled fluid syneresis. We introduce three biomimetic fabrication concepts derived from human anatomy: (1) Volumetric Syneresis Printing (Z-axis Collapse) via tension-induced fluid efflux guided by specific mold geometries; (2) Self-Routing by Exclusion for the automated embedding of micro-circuits, utilizing mechanical resistance and bending stiffness to prevent buckling; and (3) Monolithic Gliding-Plane Fabrication (Mechanical Pruning) via non-invasive, localized low-frequency shear stress (e.g., acoustic radiation). This PCT-driven approach offers a paradigm shift from top-down spatial deposition to bottom-up, physics-driven self-assembly, unlocking new manufacturing capabilities for soft robotics, tissue engineering, and smart materials.
